title: Teacher training in the age of AI: Impact on AI Literacy and Teachers' Attitudes
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an online professional development program can improve in-service teachers’ AI literacy, AI-related usage behaviors, and attitudes toward AI in education. The motivation is that teachers are increasingly expected both to use AI in their own work and to prepare students for an AI-shaped society, yet many teachers report limited preparation and uncertainty about how to integrate AI responsibly into teaching.

The intervention studied was a four-week online certificate course, “Artificial Intelligence in Everyday School and Classroom Practice,” offered through the fobizz platform. The course combined synchronous and asynchronous elements, including a kickoff webinar, a mandatory self-paced module, optional modules on topics such as machine learning, ethics, inclusive education, and data protection, plus live webinars/workshops and a final project in which participants created an AI-supported lesson plan. The study used a pre-post design with no control group, administering an objective AI literacy test to 291 teachers and an attitudes questionnaire to 436 participants across three course iterations.

Participants were primarily German in-service teachers from a variety of school types, though the course also attracted individuals from adult education, higher education, and school administration. The setting was fully online. The study found statistically significant improvements in overall AI literacy and in 10 of 14 AI literacy competency areas, though effect sizes were generally small. Attitudes and self-reported usage showed stronger gains: participants reported more frequent AI use in daily life and teaching tasks, greater willingness to integrate AI into practice, and substantially stronger feelings of preparedness to use AI in teaching.

The authors conclude that structured teacher training can support AI integration in education by improving both knowledge and confidence. At the same time, they note that teachers still answered only about half of the AI literacy items correctly after the program, suggesting persistent knowledge gaps. The paper argues for continued and possibly more specialized teacher AI training, education-specific AI literacy assessments, and future longitudinal research to test whether these gains persist and transfer into classroom practice.

identified_tools.name: fobizz AI Assistant
identified_tools.description: An AI feature within the fobizz professional development platform used to support classroom-related planning and material creation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by in-service teachers during a four-week online training program to develop AI-supported lesson plans and explore AI use in classroom practice.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers’ overall AI literacy improved significantly from pre-test to post-test after the training program that included use of fobizz AI tools. Mean AI literacy scores increased from 13.15 (SD 5.46) to 15.13 (SD 5.14), with p < 0.001 and a small effect size of d = 0.37 (N₁ = 291).
findings.measure: Validated AI literacy test total score

findings.finding_summary: Ten of 14 AI literacy competencies showed statistically significant gains following the training. Significant improvements were reported for Recognizing AI (d = 0.17, p = 0.005), Interdisciplinarity (d = 0.27, p < .001), General vs. Narrow AI (d = 0.20, p < .001), AI's Strengths and Weaknesses (d = 0.23, p < .001), Representations (d = 0.26, p < .001), Decision-Making (d = 0.25, p < .001), ML Steps (d = 0.30, p < .001), Human Role in AI (d = 0.19, p = 0.007), Critically Interpreting Data (d = 0.13, p = 0.044), and Ethics (d = 0.20, p = 0.001).

Teachers reported significantly greater AI use and readiness for integration after the training. Mean agreement increased for regular AI use in daily life from 1.37 to 2.28 (d = 1.07), use of AI for lesson/material creation from 1.27 to 2.35 (d = 1.32), use for assessment/grading from 0.41 to 1.04 (d = 0.67), imagining AI integration into teaching from 2.45 to 2.72 (d = 0.49), and feeling well-prepared to integrate AI from 1.03 to 2.28 (d = 1.65), all p < 0.001 (N₂ = 436).
findings.measure: Teacher attitude items on AI use and preparedness (4-point Likert items I1, I2, I3, I5, I8)

findings.finding_summary: Teachers’ beliefs about AI in education changed significantly in both positive and cautionary directions after the program. Agreement increased that AI offers an opportunity to support students (I6: 2.39 to 2.67, d = 0.50, p < 0.001), but also increased on items indicating concern that AI in schools is more of a threat than an opportunity (I4: 0.98 to 1.37, d = 0.42, p < 0.001) and that AI will replace teachers in the future (I7: 0.45 to 0.67, d = 0.25, p < 0.001) (N₂ = 436).
findings.measure: Teacher belief items on AI opportunities and risks in education (4-point Likert items I4, I6, I7)

quality_tier_rationale: This is a pre-post single-group intervention study without a control group, using validated and author-developed measures with statistical testing. Because it lacks randomization or a comparison condition, causal evidence is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports several medium to very large effects on teacher attitudes, use, and preparedness (e.g., d = 0.67 to 1.65), alongside a small positive effect on AI literacy (d = 0.37). Overall impact is substantial on teacher-facing outcomes.
